newsitem.title: FRANCE: Channel tunnel freight may resume - safety commission.
newsitem.headline: Channel tunnel freight may resume - safety commission.

text.p: The Channel Tunnel safety commission gave permission early on Thursday for freight trains to resume services immediately on the fire-damaged Franco-British undersea rail line, a commission member said.

Jean-Pascal Cogez, deputy prefect (government administrator) in Calais, told Reuters permission was granted for six trains to move in either direction in the tunnel every 90 minutes. The tunnel has been closed since a fire on a truck transporter train on Monday night.
A decision on when freight trains would effectively resume service was up to Eurotunnel SA Plc, the operators of the tunnel, and the railway companies involved, Cogez said.
Eurotunnel's operations manager, Alain Bertrand, earlier said he hoped freight trains might resume within hours.

Cogez quoted a communique by the 12-member safety commission, which held a lengthy meeting in the Channel port of Calais through Wednesday evening, which said: "The security commission does not oppose a resumption of this (freight) type of traffic."
The commission said it now expected proposals from operators about resumption of passenger and other services.

The commission said it had decided to give authorisation for freight trains to begin moving again after receiving assurances about security measures and equipment in the parts of the tunnel that will be used.
The channel tunnel is made up of separate tunnels handling north-south and south-north traffic with a third service tunnel in between. The three tunnels are linked by junction points.

Freight trains were cleared to move through the through the undamaged portion of the France-to-Britain tunnel, then transferring through a junction point to the Britain-to-France tunnel which was entirely clear for operations, the commission said.

Bertrand earlier told radio station France-Info-Frequence Nord that he hoped Eurostar passenger trains and shuttle trains carrying private cars and their passengers in the 51-km (32-mile) tunnel might start rolling again before the end of the week.
Bertrand's statement contradicted a statement by the French SNCF railways which indicated passenger services would not resume until next week.

An SNCF statement said: "Taking account of the prolonged closure of the Channel Tunnel, the Eurostar (rail) service is completely suspended for an as yet undetermined period, which ought to include the weekend of November 23-24.
He gave no indication when shuttle trains carrying cargo lorries would resume services.
It was a fire on one such lorry-carrying shuttle train which unleashed a storm of criticism of much-vaunted safety systems and resulted in all traffic being suspended.
Main roads in and around Calais were congested late on Wednesday with heavy lorries which would normally have used the tunnel but were trying to embark on cross-channel ferry vessels.

Eurotunnel said damage in the tunnel was worse than first feared with buckled tracks, cracked concrete and damage to electrical cables. Full repairs are likely to last weeks and cost millions of pounds (dollars).

The only trains which ran in the tunnel on Wednesday were shuttling staff -- the closure to paying clients means a loss of revenues of about a million pounds ($1.7 million) a day, a pinprick compared to the company's nine billion pounds ($15 billion) in debts.
